approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would change workplace bargaining rules to encourage talks about making businesses more efficient.

It would require the Fair Work Commission to check that productivity improvements were discussed before approving most enterprise agreements, and to consider several factors when deciding whether to allow a strike ballot.
The Commission would also have to refuse a strike ballot if the applicant's demands are clearly excessive or would seriously hurt workplace productivity.
Adds a new condition for approving enterprise agreements that are not greenfields agreements.
Requires the Fair Work Commission to consider a list of factors when assessing if an applicant is genuinely trying to reach an agreement.
Prevents the Fair Work Commission from ordering a protected action ballot if the applicant's claims are manifestly excessive or would significantly harm productivity.
Employers, employees and unions involved in enterprise bargaining under the Fair Work Act.

Opposed the Fair Work Amendment (Bargaining Processes) Bill 2014 and moved its referral to a Senate committee, arguing that its ambiguous productivity and protected industrial action provisions could add red tape, increase costs, create uncertainty and shift bargaining power toward employers.

Supported the Fair Work Amendment (Bargaining Processes) Bill 2014, citing research on six Western Australian minimum wage increases between 1994 and 2001 that found youth employment fell nearly three times faster than overall employment, and said youth unemployment rose from 9 per cent in January 2008 to 12.4 per cent by the end of 2013 under Labor.

Opposed the Fair Work Amendment (Bargaining Processes) Bill 2014 as an attack on the right to collectively bargain and strike, noting 63 per cent of Work Choices era workplace agreements removed penalty rates, and cited Reserve Bank Governor Glenn Stevens' observation that labour productivity is growing at about 2 per cent a year under the Fair Work Act.

Supported the Fair Work Amendment (Bargaining Processes) Bill 2014, citing more than 750 new jobs generated by the Geelong Region Innovation and Investment Fund and the rollout of the NBN to 34,000 premises in Corangamite, and described unlawful CFMEU conduct on the Regional Rail Link project that cost Boral $10 million.

Supported the Fair Work Amendment (Bargaining Processes) Bill 2014, arguing it would end a strike-first-talk-later approach to industrial action, and cited the member for Hume's opinion article arguing productivity is a worker's best friend, drawing on research by the member for Fraser.

Opposed the Fair Work Amendment Bargaining Processes Bill as a broken election promise that adds red tape and lets the Fair Work Commission block protected action ballots it judges excessive, arguing it is designed to suppress workers' wages and conditions rather than genuinely improve productivity.

Opened debate on the Fair Work Amendment (Bargaining Processes) Bill 2014, noting that 39 government backbenchers, about two-thirds of the backbench, had declined that morning to endorse the government's policy direction at a party room meeting.

Opposed the Fair Work Amendment (Bargaining Processes) Bill 2014, challenging the minister's second reading speech claim that marine engineers in Port Hedland sought a 38 per cent pay rise over four years when the dispute was reportedly settled at zero, two, two and two per cent, and said 83 per cent of mining and resources profits go overseas.

Supported the Fair Work Amendment (Bargaining Processes) Bill 2014, arguing productivity discussion requirements would help address a budget position where government spends $110 million a day more than it raises, and compared interest paid per citizen on debt, finding Australia's $900 a year higher than the $736 paid per person in Greece.

Closed debate on the Fair Work Amendment (Bargaining Processes) Bill 2014, rejecting claims it would add red tape, and cited Department of Employment data showing about 48 per cent of enterprise agreements approved between January 2010 and June 2014 already contain productivity commitment clauses.
